what: Prices the fixed per-transaction cost of SQLite commit at the product's own pragma profile, holding bytes constant. It does NOT run the product and cannot attribute the product's commit_ns; it bounds what a cadence change could remove.
method: Copy the row's base.sqlite; apply PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY, synchronous=OFF, temp_store=MEMORY, foreign_keys=ON (the product profile, sqlite/connection.rs:32-48); insert identical 32 KiB blobs into object_packs until 268,435,456 bytes have been written; vary only the number of BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT pairs. One sample per arm.

derived.note: Fixed per-transaction cost from the extremes: (550620792-444408875)/(8192-74) = 13084 ns. From the middle segment: (454763917-444408875)/(1366-74) = 7959 ns. The two disagree because the relationship is not linear over this range and each arm is one sample; both are reported.

conclusion: A ~238x reduction in transaction count at constant bytes saves at most ~6.4% of this row's operation on this replica. The product's measured 77,762.7 ns per commit is ~5.9x the ~13.1 us fixed cost, so the majority of commit_ns is page-flush work proportional to the bytes written, which batching does not remove. Cadence is real but is NOT the 38.2% lever its share suggests.
caveat: One sample per arm, synthetic replica, a single table, no secondary indexes, no foreign keys exercised on the written table, and only 8,192 rows. It bounds the cadence term; it does not decompose the product's commit_ns.
